title: Recursive Language Models
claim: A baseline degrades sharply with input length and task complexity, while our method stays strong, even beyond the baseline's context limit.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared axes, red vs green shaded out-of-context region
description: Two side-by-side line charts with the same axes. The x-axis is input context length on a log scale, from 8k to 1M tokens. The y-axis is score in percent, from 0 to 100. The left panel is titled GPT-5 and uses blue lines with markers. The S-NIAH line stays flat at 100. The OOLONG line falls from about 92 to 31. The OOLONG-Pairs line collapses to about 0 by 33k. A pink shaded region on the right marks lengths beyond the context window, and its x-labels are red. The right panel is titled RLM(GPT-5) and uses orange lines. S-NIAH stays at 100. OOLONG and OOLONG-Pairs decline gently, staying around 45 to 60 even at 1M. A green shaded region marks lengths the baseline cannot handle. The eye goes first to the contrast between the collapsing blue curves and the stable orange curves.
caption: A comparison of GPT-5 and a corresponding RLM(recursion depth=1) using GPT-5 on three long-context tasks of increasing complexity: S-NIAH, OOLONG, and OOLONG-Pairs. For each task, we scale the input length from 213 to 220. GPT-5 performance degrades significantly as a function of both input length and task complexity, while the RLM maintains strong performance. Inputs beyond the red region do not fit in GPT-5’s context window of 272K tokens, but the RLM handles them effectively. Additional experiments across other models and benchmarks are in §3.
abstract: We study allowing large language models (LLMs) to process arbitrarily long prompts through the lens of inference-time scaling. We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt. We find that RLMs can successfully process inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows and, even for shorter prompts, dramatically outperform the quality of vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context and coding scaffolds (e.g., on GPT-5 by a median across the evaluated benchmarks of $26\%$ against compaction, $130\%$ against CodeAct with sub-calls, and $13\%$ against Claude Code) across four diverse long-context tasks while having comparable cost. At a small scale, we post-train the first model around the RLM. Our model, RLM-Qwen3-8B, outperforms the underlying Qwen3-8B model by $28.3\%$ on average and even approaches the quality of vanilla GPT-5 on three long-context tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/alexzhang13/rlm.
